analysis.one_liner: Lets businesses deduct the full cost of new equipment immediately instead of writing it off over years.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change a tax rule called Section 179, which normally lets small businesses deduct only a limited dollar amount of new equipment purchases right away. For equipment placed in service between September 8, 2010, and January 1, 2012, the bill would remove those limits entirely, letting any business deduct 100% of the cost of depreciable assets immediately. The federal government would collect less tax in the short run on the theory that faster write-offs encourage businesses to buy equipment now.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses buying depreciable assets in the covered window — especially larger ones, since removing the dollar cap helps firms with big capital budgets far more than small firms bumping against the old limit. They get the full tax deduction up front instead of spreading it over years, which improves cash flow and lowers their near-term tax bill. Equipment sellers could also benefit if the immediate write-off nudges buyers to purchase sooner.

how_it_helps.text: For property placed in service on or after September 8, 2010, and before January 1, 2012, the bill suspends the dollar limits on Section 179 expensing, so a business can deduct the entire cost of qualifying assets in the year of purchase rather than depreciating over time.
For the portion of the tax year before September 8, 2010, the existing dollar limits would be prorated by days, and the new rules apply to property placed in service in that window.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury: every dollar deducted up front instead of over time is tax revenue the government does not collect in the near term, a cost ultimately shared by all taxpayers. The bill contains no offsetting revenue provision.

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces federal revenue with no offset, and immediate expensing mostly rewards purchases businesses would have made anyway, so its cost buys little new investment.

The bill is aimed at businesses with large capital budgets; removing the dollar cap does almost nothing for the smallest firms that the Section 179 limit was designed to help, while delivering the largest write-offs to the biggest buyers.

The bill as written contains a drafting error: the effective-date clause applies to property placed in service 'on or after September 31, 2010' — a date that does not exist — leaving the start of the special expensing period technically ambiguous.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster cash flow for businesses that buy equipment, which might modestly pull purchases forward into a weak economy. The cost is lost federal revenue in the near term, and the removal of the dollar cap means most of that cost flows to the largest purchasers rather than the small businesses the existing rule favors. As drafted, it also contains a date error that would need fixing in any future version. On balance, this is a straightforward business tax cut whose public benefit is speculative and whose cost is concrete.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi introduced the bill on September 15, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the last action the bill ever received.
It drew a single cosponsor and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers are better off, since the near-term revenue cost of unlimited expensing was never incurred; businesses hoping for the write-off are worse off.

for.name: Rep. John Garamendi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: 1 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it ever had.

against.name: Rep. Sander Levin
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or a vote; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor were House Democrats, and no vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how either party would have lined up.

industries.note: They would have gained the largest write-offs under the bill, and the bill's death means they do not. Their gain under the bill — lower near-term taxes with no offset — would have been paid for by all federal taxpayers.
Immediate expensing is designed to pull equipment purchases forward, which could have boosted their sales; with the bill dead, that stimulus never arrived.
